title: Gadget plays: the wildcat, the halfback pass and the pitch
html:
Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this morning: it still holds only one logged game (Eagles at Bears, Week 3, 0 saved snaps) and no review files, and the original football-film-room repository was again not reachable from this run (access denied: not configured for this session). So there's no new miss of yours to fix, and no snap of yours this connects to yet. It takes a new concept from this weekend instead: three games turned on plays where someone other than the quarterback handled the ball in an unusual way. These are also the plays most likely to fool a pre-snap run/pass call in your drill.

The big idea: most plays are built on the defense knowing who gets the snap (the quarterback) and who can throw (also the quarterback). Gadget plays break one of those two assumptions on purpose. They work because defenses play their tendencies: linebackers fly toward a run, safeties fill in. Used once or twice a game, at the right moment, they get a free touchdown. Overused, the defense waits for them.

White = offense, yellow = defense; the yellow-filled circle is the player with the ball. Top: the wildcat. Bottom: a halfback pass after a pitch.

  1. The wildcat (top of the diagram). The center snaps the ball straight to a running back or receiver lined up about 5 yards deep, and the quarterback lines up wide as a decoy. Why it works: on a normal handoff, the quarterback hands off and stops playing, so the run game is effectively 10 offensive players against 11 defenders. In the wildcat, the runner is the player taking the snap, so every offensive player is a blocker or the runner: 11 against 11. Saturday at South Carolina, Tennessee trailed 17-14 in the second quarter when receiver Mike Matthews took a wildcat snap and ran 8 yards for the touchdown that gave the Vols their first lead, 21-17. (South Carolina's Vicari Swain was also ejected in that half for targeting Matthews.)
  2. The halfback pass (bottom). The quarterback hands or pitches to the running back, who starts running toward the sideline. The linebackers and a safety come up to stop the run (the same trick as play-action, Lesson 16), and the back stops and throws to a receiver behind them. Any player can throw a forward pass, as long as he's behind the line of scrimmage and it's the only forward pass of the play. Friday night at Virginia, Duke running back Nate Sheppard threw a 28-yard touchdown pass with about a minute left: Duke 19, Virginia 16, the winning score.
  3. The pitch, and why it's risky. A pitch (a soft toss to a back running wide, the heart of the option, Lesson 21) travels backward, so it's a backward pass: if it hits the ground, it's a live fumble, and the defense can recover it (Lesson 29: loose balls are live). Michigan's Tommy Carr, making his first start, lost a fumble on a bad pitch in the first quarter against Indiana, one of his two turnovers in a 13-6 overtime loss.
  4. When coaches call them. Near the goal line (where the extra blocker of the wildcat matters most, Lesson 17), late in close games (Duke), and right after a big emotional moment, when a defense is playing fast and aggressive. A team with a running quarterback gets some of the same "11 against 11" math on every play; that's why Lesson 33's designed quarterback runs are so hard to stop.
  5. The rule that kills gadget passes: offensive linemen can't be more than 1 yard downfield in the NFL (3 yards in college) when a forward pass is thrown beyond the line. On a halfback pass, linemen are run-blocking, so they drift downfield: a flag for ineligible man downfield wipes out the play (Lesson 13 covers penalties).

How to log it in your drill: log what the formation tells you before the snap. A wildcat look (no quarterback under center or in the shotgun, a back or receiver deep) is a RUN call; it is a run the large majority of the time. A halfback pass will be scored PASS, so a RUN call on it will show as a miss: that's the play doing its job, not a mistake in your rule. Keep calling RUN on those looks. One clue that helps: a running back lined up deep with an unusually wide split by the receiver on the side he's running away from.

Real examples to look for: the rest of Saturday night (Ole Miss at Texas, Sun 8:30 a.m. JST / Sat 4:30 p.m. PT, ABC) and Sunday's NFL games inside the 5-yard line, where direct snaps to running backs show up most. Monday night, Philadelphia with backup Tanner McKee (Tue 9:15 a.m. JST / Mon 5:15 p.m. PT, ESPN/ABC) is the kind of offense that adds a trick play or two to make up for a backup quarterback.

Video: search YouTube for "wildcat formation explained," "halfback pass touchdown," and "Duke Virginia Nate Sheppard touchdown pass," and "Tennessee South Carolina Mike Matthews wildcat touchdown."

Practice it in Football Camp → (Station 5: Plays)

quiz.q: In a wildcat formation, who takes the snap?
o: A running back or receiver lined up a few yards deep
quiz.w: The snap goes straight to a runner (Tennessee used receiver Mike Matthews), and the quarterback lines up wide as a decoy.

quiz.q: Why does the wildcat help the run game?
o: The runner takes the snap, so no offensive player is 'wasted' handing off: 11 vs. 11
quiz.w: On a normal handoff the quarterback stops playing after the handoff. In the wildcat every offensive player blocks or carries the ball.

quiz.q: Duke's Nate Sheppard, a running back, threw the winning TD at Virginia. Is that legal?
o: Yes, any player may throw one forward pass from behind the line of scrimmage
Only if he's a former quarterback
quiz.w: Any player can throw a forward pass, as long as it's from behind the line of scrimmage and it's the only forward pass on the play.

quiz.q: Tommy Carr's pitch hit the ground and Indiana recovered. Why was it a fumble and not an incomplete pass?
o: A pitch goes backward, so it's a backward pass: a ball on the ground is live
Because it was the first quarter
quiz.w: Only an incomplete forward pass is dead. A backward pass (a pitch or lateral) that hits the ground is a live ball that either team can recover.

quiz.q: In your drill, a team lines up in a wildcat look. What should you call?
o: RUN, even though a halfback pass is possible
PASS if it's third down, always
quiz.w: Call RUN: wildcat looks are runs most of the time. If it turns out to be a gadget pass, that 'miss' is the play working as designed; keep your rule.
